title: Powered flight
matchup: The Wright brothers (1903) vs Giffard (1852) and Ader (1890)
question: Does Giffard's 1852 airship flight support Schmidhuber's objection to calling the Wrights' 1903 flights the first powered, controlled and sustained flights?

usual_credit.summary: The Wright brothers are conventionally credited with the first successful powered, controlled flight of a heavier-than-air machine, rather than the first ascent in any powered aircraft. The [Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum](https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/wright-brothers-made-history-kitty-hawk) uses that qualified description for their December 1903 flights and explains the glider experiments and control system behind them. This distinction matters because an airship obtains lift from buoyancy, whereas an airplane must generate aerodynamic lift.

works.title: The Wright Flyer flights at Kitty Hawk, 17 December 1903 (Smithsonian historical account)

claim.summary: Schmidhuber objects to descriptions that drop the heavier-than-air qualification and call the Wrights' achievement simply the first powered, controlled and sustained flight. He identifies Henri Giffard's steam-powered dirigible as an earlier example, and also cites Clément Ader's 1890 machine when discussing heavier-than-air experiments. His 2003 Nature letter nevertheless explicitly credits the Wrights with combining a human pilot, power, heavier-than-air flight and control, so his correction is not a denial of that more specific achievement.

response.summary: The [Smithsonian](https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/wright-brothers-made-history-kitty-hawk) credits the Wrights with powered, controlled heavier-than-air flight, while the [Science Museum](https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co29385/the-giffard-airship) credits Giffard with the first successful application of mechanical power to flight. The latter also says his airship could not navigate a circle against the wind and return, which qualifies its control. Schmidhuber's 2003 letter itself credits the Wrights with the conjunction of powered, manned, heavier-than-air and controlled flight. These accounts distinguish the milestones without establishing Ader's machine as an equivalent of the Wrights' controlled airplane, and do not constitute direct replies to his letters.

quotes.text: They made the first powered, controlled flight of a heavier-than-air flying machine.
the airship lacked the power to navigate a circle against the wind and return to its starting point.

agreed_facts: Giffard flew a steam-powered dirigible on 24 September 1852: https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co29385/the-giffard-airship
The Wrights flew their powered airplane at Kitty Hawk on 17 December 1903: https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/wright-brothers-made-history-kitty-hawk
Schmidhuber's 2003 Nature letter credits the Wrights with a conjunction of manned, powered, heavier-than-air and controlled flight: https://www.nature.com/articles/421689c
crux: The central issue is the wording of the claimed first: all powered flight, powered airship flight, or powered and controlled heavier-than-air flight. Giffard's earlier airship can challenge the unqualified description without establishing priority for the airplane achievement recognized by the Smithsonian.

card.headline: First powered flight
card.question: Does Giffard's 1852 airship beat the Wrights to the first powered, controlled, sustained flight?
card.claim: He says Giffard's steam airship made the first powered, controlled, sustained flight in 1852, though he credits the Wrights for heavier-than-air flight.
card.pushback: The Science Museum says Giffard's airship lacked the power to circle against the wind and return, so its control was limited.
card.crux: The question is whether "first powered flight" should include airships or mean controlled flight in a heavier-than-air machine.
